chapters.file: ch04 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
ch05 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: The editor's introduction frames the whole collection around three topics in Burton's corpus—identity, authority, and aesthetics—and previews each essay. On identity it contrasts an essentialist "core self" with an empirical, experience-built self, using Big Fish and Batman Returns as test cases; on authority it surveys Mars Attacks!, Sleepy Hollow, and Batman; on aesthetics it points to Sweeney Todd, death, and color. It functions as a roadmap that argues Burton's films merit philosophical reading rather than advancing one philosopher's thesis.

chapters.file: ch06 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
ch07 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: Ken Hada argues that Big Fish dramatizes a narrative, intersubjective account of the self against essentialist and Cartesian views. Dying storyteller Ed Bloom builds his identity through fantastic tales (the giant catfish, the Witch), while his journalist son Will—who dismisses the stories as lies—illustrates a 'circumscribed self' that refuses the social shaping every self undergoes. Drawing on Sartre's consciousness-as-nothingness and 'the Other teaches who I am,' Mead's generalized other, Aboulafia's mediating self, and Benjamin's 'The Storyteller,' Hada reads Will's climactic act of telling his father's death-scene as his becoming a mediating storyteller and granting Ed narrative immortality. Hume's 'bundle'/self-as-fiction and Descartes' cogito are invoked as the poles Ed's storied self transcends.

chapters.file: ch08 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: Ryan Weldon reads Selina Kyle's transformation into Catwoman in Batman Returns through Sartre's existentialism and Beauvoir's The Second Sex. Pre-death Selina is Sartre's inauthentic 'waiter,' performing a servile secretary role in bad faith, and Beauvoir's objectified Other, defined by Max Shreck and the men who dismiss her. Her murder and feline resurrection free repressed drives, and her refusal of Batman's fairy-tale rescue—'I couldn't live with myself'—plus her choice to kill Shreck are cast as an assertion of facticity and transcendence, an authentic (if unfinished) self-creation that rejects the roles available to women rather than reaching a stable ending.

chapters.file: ch09 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: Daniel Sullivan argues that Burton and Poe channel childhood 'ontological insecurity' (R. D. Laing) into horror fantasy, using Burton's short Vincent as case study. Seven-year-old Vincent Malloy, imagining himself as Vincent Price, escapes 'necessity's despair' into fantastic possibility but slides into what Kierkegaard's Sickness unto Death calls defiant then demonic despair, clinging to a self-as-victim identity until he collapses. Sullivan reads fantasy as both consolation and danger—the flight into possibility further isolates the insecure child—and extends the possibility/necessity dialectic and Otto Rank's life/creation dialectic to Nightmare Before Christmas, Edward Scissorhands, and Big Fish.

chapters.file: ch10 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: Mark Walling argues that the appeal of Burton-Depp characters lies in a recovered model of childhood consciousness. Against Freud's and Piaget's view that children perceive less and are locked in the here-and-now, Walling uses Alison Gopnik's cognitive science ('babies are more conscious than we are') and Rousseau's romantic ideal of the naturally good, untutored child to read Edward Scissorhands and Ed Wood. Edward is a naturally gifted, innocent artist destroyed by a corrupt suburban 'society'; Ed Wood, megaphone in hand, is 'an eight-year-old who wants to be a movie director,' whose inattentional, make-believe joy in filmmaking—not the finished product—embodies the wide, wondering child mind Burton celebrates.

chapters.file: ch11 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
ch12 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: Paul A. Cantor argues that Mars Attacks! inverts the pro-government ideology of 1950s flying-saucer films (Earth vs. the Flying Saucers, Invaders from Mars, The Day the Earth Stood Still) in which scientific and military elites save a helpless public. Burton instead mocks Washington's vain, media-obsessed, multicultural establishment—Kessler, President Dale, the generals—who all fail, while Kansas 'trailer trash,' a Las Vegas boxer, and truant video-gaming kids improvise the defense; Slim Whitman's yodeling, not the state, defeats the Martians. Cantor reads the film through Tocqueville's Democracy in America on the self-organizing power of citizens' associations and the danger of soft despotism, and against Hobbes/The Day the Earth Stood Still's Leviathan solution, casting Burton as a Tocquevillian celebrant of ordinary Americans over their governing elite.

chapters.file: ch13 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: Steve Benton reads Burton's Sleepy Hollow as a meditation on rationality and anti-intellectualism, contrasting it with Washington Irving's original where brainy Ichabod is run out of town. Burton's Ichabod, a rationalist constable, prevails only after tempering his faith in science with emotion, intuition, and the spirit world associated with his mother and Katrina—the paper-disk toy (bird/cage) symbolizing how head and heart must spin together. Benton maps the film's models of rationality onto Plato's philosopher-king and distrust of the mob and Hobbes's war of all against all (Burton's corrupt New York and Sleepy Hollow) versus the collaborative, democratic reason of Locke, Mill's On Liberty, and Dewey, invoking Aristotle and Nussbaum on emotion's role in practical wisdom; he leaves open whether the film is transgressive or a conventional 'woman heals cold rational man' Hollywood tale.

chapters.file: ch14 - The Philosophy of Tim Burton.md
chapters.relation: Kevin S. Decker offers a 'philosophical hermeneutics' of Burton's Batman and Batman Returns, arguing that a long-lived cultural artifact like the Batman discloses a society's self-understanding. Using Heidegger's Dasein and 'working-out of possibilities,' Nietzsche's 'only interpretations,' and Gadamer's hermeneutic circle and fusion of horizons, Decker reads the shift from ABC's camp Adam West Batman to Burton's dark version as tracking cultural change (Vietnam, Watergate, 1980s decadence). He casts the Joker, Penguin, and Catwoman—and Batman himself—as Burton's recurring 'expressive outsider,' relating them to Nietzsche's Übermensch and Gotham's gullible crowds to Heidegger's das Man, and compares Burton's Expressionist Gotham to Max Beckmann's post-WWI Hell lithographs, positioning Burton as a prophet of modern decadence.

holes.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
holes.what: Nineteenth-century French political thinker whose Democracy in America analyzed American self-government, the citizens' 'art of association,' and the risk of a centralizing 'soft despotism.'
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire argument reads Mars Attacks! through Tocqueville's Democracy in America—the self-organizing power of ordinary Americans versus reliance on the federal government—and the taxonomy has no Tocqueville slug and no adequate substitute.
